title: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Hydrocarbons

questions.chapter: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Hydrocarbons
questions.q: The number of structural isomers of $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$ is:
questions.solution:
Butane has **two** structural isomers:

**n-butane**, a straight chain of four carbons, and **isobutane** (2-methylpropane), a three-carbon chain with a methyl branch.

There is no third arrangement: putting the methyl on carbon 1 or 3 just regenerates n-butane.

Pentane has three isomers and hexane five, so the count grows quickly after this.

questions.chapter: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Hydrocarbons
questions.q: Which group shows a $+\text{I}$ (electron-releasing inductive) effect?
questions.solution:
An alkyl group such as $\mathbf{-\text{CH}_3}$ **releases** electron density through the sigma framework, a $+\text{I}$ effect.

The other three are electronegative or electron-withdrawing and show $-\text{I}$.

This is why more substituted carbocations are more stable — each alkyl group pushes electron density towards the positive centre — and it underlies Markovnikov's rule.

questions.chapter: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Hydrocarbons
questions.q: The order of stability of carbocations is:
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ > \text{methyl}}$.

Two effects work together. Each attached alkyl group releases electron density through the $+\text{I}$ effect, stabilising the positive charge; and **hyperconjugation** delocalises it further, with more alpha C-H bonds available the more substituted the carbon is.

A tertiary carbocation has nine such hydrogens, a methyl cation none.

Note that for **carbanions** the order is exactly reversed, since electron release destabilises a negative charge.

questions.chapter: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Hydrocarbons
questions.q: Markovnikov's rule states that in the addition of HX to an unsymmetrical alkene, the hydrogen adds to the carbon with:
questions.solution:
The hydrogen goes to the carbon already bearing **more hydrogens** — the popular phrasing being that the rich get richer.

The real reason is the **stability of the intermediate carbocation**: adding $\text{H}^{+}$ to the less substituted carbon leaves the positive charge on the more substituted one, which is the more stable cation.

In the presence of peroxides, HBr alone adds the other way round, via a free-radical mechanism — the anti-Markovnikov or Kharasch effect.

questions.chapter: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Hydrocarbons
questions.q: According to Huckel's rule, an aromatic compound must have:
options: $(4n+2)$ pi electrons in a planar cyclic conjugated system
questions.solution:
Huckel's rule requires $(4n+2)$ delocalised pi electrons in a **planar, cyclic, fully conjugated** ring, with $n = 0, 1, 2 \ldots$

Benzene has 6 pi electrons ($n = 1$) and is aromatic. Cyclobutadiene has 4 and is **antiaromatic** and highly unstable.

All three structural conditions matter, not just the count: cyclooctatetraene has 8 pi electrons and avoids antiaromaticity by puckering into a tub shape, so it is simply non-aromatic.

questions.chapter: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Hydrocarbons
options: In one step, with inversion of configuration
questions.solution:
$\text{S}_\text{N}2$ is a **single concerted step**: the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the leaving group as that group departs.

The result is **inversion of configuration**, known as Walden inversion — the molecule turns inside out like an umbrella in the wind.

It is fastest on **methyl and primary** halides, where the back side is unhindered, and essentially does not occur on tertiary ones. $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ is the tertiary route, going through a planar carbocation and giving racemisation.

questions.chapter: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Hydrocarbons
questions.q: Terminal alkynes are weakly acidic because the C-H bond involves carbon that is:
questions.solution:
A terminal alkyne carbon is **$sp$** hybridised, so its bonding orbital has $50\%$ s-character.

An s orbital holds electrons closer to the nucleus, so the carbanion left behind when the proton leaves is more stable — and the C-H bond is correspondingly more acidic.

Acidity therefore follows the s-character: $sp\ (50\%) > sp^{2}\ (33\%) > sp^{3}\ (25\%)$, that is alkyne > alkene > alkane.

It is still very weakly acidic — around $\text{p}K_a\ 25$ — but enough to form acetylides with sodamide, which is a useful way of building longer carbon chains.

questions.chapter: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Hydrocarbons
questions.q: A compound that rotates plane-polarised light must contain:
options: A chiral centre or be otherwise non-superimposable on its mirror image
questions.solution:
Optical activity requires **chirality**: the molecule must not be superimposable on its mirror image.

The usual cause is a carbon bearing **four different groups**, but it is not the only one — allenes and some biphenyls are chiral without any such centre, which is why the condition is stated as non-superimposability rather than as a count of chiral centres.

A molecule with chiral centres can still be optically **inactive** if it has an internal plane of symmetry: that is a **meso** compound.

questions.chapter: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Hydrocarbons
questions.q: Benzene undergoes electrophilic **substitution** rather than addition because:
questions.solution:
Addition would destroy the delocalised pi system and forfeit benzene's **resonance stabilisation** of roughly $150\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

**Substitution** restores aromaticity once the proton is lost, so the ring survives intact — which is why it is strongly preferred.

Benzene can be made to undergo addition under forcing conditions, such as hydrogenation with a nickel catalyst at high temperature and pressure, but it is not its characteristic reaction.

questions.chapter: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Hydrocarbons
questions.q: How many structural isomers does $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}$ have?
questions.solution:
Pentane has $\mathbf{3}$ structural isomers:

**n-pentane**, a straight chain of five carbons

**isopentane** (2-methylbutane), a four-carbon chain with one methyl branch

**neopentane** (2,2-dimethylpropane), a three-carbon chain with two methyls on the middle carbon

questions.chapter: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Hydrocarbons
questions.q: A molecule has 2 chiral centres and no internal symmetry. How many optical isomers does it have?
questions.solution:
The maximum number of optical isomers is $2^{n}$, where $n$ is the number of chiral centres.

$2^{2} = \mathbf{4}$ — two pairs of enantiomers.

The count is reduced when the molecule has internal symmetry, because a **meso** form makes two of the notional isomers identical. Tartaric acid is the classic example: two chiral centres but only three distinct stereoisomers.

questions.chapter: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Hydrocarbons
questions.q: How many moles of $\text{O}_2$ are needed for the complete combustion of 1 mole of propane, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8$?
questions.solution:
$\text{C}_3\text{H}_8 + 5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 3\text{CO}_2 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$

Balancing: 3 carbons need $3\text{CO}_2$, 8 hydrogens need $4\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Total oxygen atoms on the right $= 6 + 4 = 10$, so $\mathbf{5}$ moles of $\text{O}_2$.

questions.chapter: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Hydrocarbons
questions.q: What is the degree of unsaturation of a compound with molecular formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6$?
questions.solution:
Degree of unsaturation $= \dfrac{2C + 2 - H}{2}$

$= \dfrac{2(6) + 2 - 6}{2} = \dfrac{12 + 2 - 6}{2} = \dfrac{8}{2} = \mathbf{4}$.

For benzene that is one ring plus three double bonds, which is exactly right.

questions.chapter: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Hydrocarbons
questions.q: How many alpha hydrogens are available for hyperconjugation in the tertiary butyl carbocation, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^{+}$?
questions.solution:
The positive carbon carries three methyl groups, and each methyl has three hydrogens on the carbon **alpha** to the cationic centre.

$3 \times 3 = \mathbf{9}$ alpha hydrogens.

Each of those C-H sigma bonds can overlap with the empty $p$ orbital, delocalising the charge. Nine is the most available to any simple carbocation, which is why the tertiary butyl cation is so stable.

questions.chapter: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Hydrocarbons
questions.q: Compare the $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ and $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ mechanisms of nucleophilic substitution. For each, describe the steps, the kinetics, the stereochemical outcome and the effect of substrate structure, and explain why tertiary halides follow one route and primary halides the other.
questions.solution:
**$\text{S}_\text{N}2$: substitution, nucleophilic, bimolecular.**

**Steps.** A single **concerted** step. The nucleophile attacks the carbon from the side **directly opposite** the leaving group, while that group departs. The transition state has the carbon partly bonded to both, with five groups around it and the three unchanged substituents in a plane.

**Kinetics.** Both species appear in the rate-determining step, which is the only step:

$\text{rate} = k[\text{substrate}][\text{nucleophile}]$

Second order overall; doubling the nucleophile concentration doubles the rate.

**Stereochemistry.** Complete **inversion of configuration**, called Walden inversion. Because attack is necessarily from the back, the three remaining groups are pushed through, like an umbrella turning inside out in the wind. A single enantiomer gives a single enantiomer of opposite configuration.

**Substrate.** Fastest for **methyl**, then primary, then secondary. Tertiary substrates essentially do not react this way.

**$\text{S}_\text{N}1$: substitution, nucleophilic, unimolecular.**

**Steps.** Two steps.

Step 1, slow: the C-X bond breaks on its own to give a **planar carbocation** and the leaving group.

Step 2, fast: the nucleophile attacks the carbocation.

**Kinetics.** Only the substrate is involved in the slow step:

$\text{rate} = k[\text{substrate}]$

First order. Adding more nucleophile does **not** speed it up, which is the experimental signature that distinguishes the two mechanisms.

**Stereochemistry.** The carbocation is **planar** and can be attacked from either face with roughly equal probability, so an optically pure starting material gives a **racemic mixture**. In practice inversion slightly predominates, because the departing leaving group shields one face briefly before it diffuses away.

**Substrate.** Fastest for **tertiary**, then secondary, then primary. Methyl halides essentially do not react this way.

**Why the substrate decides, and the two reasons pull in opposite directions.**

The orders are exactly reversed, and that is not a coincidence — it is the same structural feature read two ways.

For **$\text{S}_\text{N}2$ the issue is steric access.** The nucleophile must reach the back side of the carbon. A tertiary carbon is surrounded by three bulky alkyl groups that physically block that approach, so the transition state is impossibly crowded. A methyl carbon has three small hydrogens and is wide open.

For **$\text{S}_\text{N}1$ the issue is carbocation stability.** The slow step creates a carbocation, so the reaction is only viable if that intermediate is reasonably stable. Alkyl groups stabilise it by the $+\text{I}$ effect and by hyperconjugation, so a tertiary cation forms readily while a primary one is far too unstable to be worth forming.

So the very alkyl groups that **block** the $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ back-side attack are the ones that **stabilise** the $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ intermediate. A tertiary halide is therefore pushed towards $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ from both directions at once, and a primary halide towards $\text{S}_\text{N}2$. Secondary halides sit in between and can go either way depending on the solvent and the nucleophile.

**Conditions that tip the balance.** A strong nucleophile and a polar **aprotic** solvent such as acetone or DMSO favour $\text{S}_\text{N}2$, since the nucleophile is left unencumbered. A weak nucleophile and a polar **protic** solvent such as water or ethanol favour $\text{S}_\text{N}1$, because the solvent stabilises the developing ions.
